newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Coles Myer announces board changes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Coles Myer announces board changes.

text.p: Australia's largest retailer Coles Myer Ltd said on Friday that Stan Wallis would become chairman from July 1997 and that it would invite Brierley Investments Ltd chief executive Paul Collins and Myer family representative Martyn Myer to join the board.

The embattled retailer also announced that as a result of the announcement that Wallis would become chairman, the board had decided that there was no need for either a deputy chairman or a vice chairman.
Former executive chairman Solomon Lew is currently deputy chairman.

Coles Myer chairman Nobby Clark said in a statement the decisions made at today's meeting would ensure the board focused on enhancing shareholder value and working productively together for the future benefit of the company.
"We have a common commitment to leadership, unity and a clear strategic direction," Clark said.
He said the board had decided to expand board membership and widen the range of skills. Shareholders would be asked to vote on seven candidates for re-election on November 19.

The board had also decided to "re-affirm the principles of its corporate governance code adopted in February 1996 and its commitment to maintaining a majority of independent directors on the board and all its committees".

The seven candidates for the board include Wallis, who was invited to fill a casual vacany in March, Dennis Eck, Coles Myer chief operating officer business units, and Nick Greiner, Solomon Lew and Peter Morgan, all of whom will retire by rotation and will stand for re-election, Clark said.
The two new candidates, Collins and Myer, would also stand for re-election.

"I strongly support the appointment of Messrs Eck, Collins and Myer as they bring relevant experience to the Board and in addition provide further representation for shareholders, I also strongly support the re-election of Messrs Lew, Greiner, Morgan and Wallis," Clark said.

Coles Myer, which accounts for almost 18 cents of every retail dollar spent in Australia, has suffered a string of management woes recently, including a bitter board room feud which led Solomon Lew to resign as executive chairman last year and a controversy over corporate governance.
The financial press has speculated that New Zealand corporate raider Brierley Investments was circling the retailer's share register after building up its near seven percent stake.
